terms.definition: the broad field of building systems that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence.
an AI subset where systems improve by learning patterns from data rather than explicit programming.
AI that creates new content (text, images, audio, video) from learned patterns instead of just analyzing existing data.
AI that forecasts future outcomes based on historical data.
AI that sorts inputs into categories by learning boundaries between classes.
AI that uncovers relationships and trends in complex datasets.
AI applying mathematical tools like regression and probability to support decisions.
neural architectures that weigh relationships between sequence elements; the basis of modern language models.
generative models that rebuild coherent data from random noise; common in image generation.
a model that compresses data to a compact form and reconstructs variations of it.
two neural networks (generator vs. discriminator) competing to produce realistic synthetic outputs.
layered networks specialized in understanding image components; used for classification.
splitting text into small units (words, parts, punctuation) for model processing.
the basic unit a language model predicts when generating text.
the instruction or question given to an AI model to guide its output.
any data supplied to the model (text, image, audio, video).
the content the model generates in response.
an adjustable setting (length, style, format, tone) shaping the output.
tailoring a model with fixed instructions, examples, approved files, or workflows for specific needs.
techniques that fine-tune or improve AI-generated content.
the iterative check-and-adjust loop used to improve model results.
producing advanced content by combining multiple input types or models.
plausible-sounding but false information invented by the model.
skewed outputs reflecting human assumptions or underrepresented groups in training data.
gaps where the training data lacked coverage of a topic or group.
visual glitches/errors in AI-generated images.
questioning and evaluating AI content instead of accepting it at face value.
how available AI tools are, depending on infrastructure, cost, and connectivity.
the observation that computing power roughly doubles about every two years.
shifts in a model's responses after updates or retraining.
training on labeled data with known correct answers.
finding structure/clusters in unlabeled data.
learning through trial and error guided by rewards and penalties.
the initial large-scale training phase on vast datasets.
the stage where a trained model generates outputs from new inputs.
